relflow learns predictions and representations from structured business data.
Describe a transaction, the history available around it, and the outcome you
want to predict. The schema defines a trainable PyTorch model.

For example, learn whether a payment will later be disputed:

```yaml
amount: 84.50
merchant: North Market
disputed: false
```

The model reads `amount` and `merchant`, and learns to predict `disputed`.
A risk team can use that prediction to prioritize payments for review.
The later dispute outcome supplies the training answer.

As the question grows, place that payment last in a **transaction sequence**
called `trxns`, after the account's earlier activity. Each transaction keeps
its booking time, amount, and merchant together. One merchant field serves
every position, and each transaction has its own dispute target.

[Build your first model →](getting-started.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Start Small

1. [Your first model](getting-started.qmd): define fields, train, and predict.
2. [Add transaction history](tutorials/transaction-history.qmd): put transactions in one `trxns` branch and predict a dispute for each one.
3. [Prepare your observations](core-concepts/binding-data.qmd): keep the same payment and history in [application-supplied Parquet files](guides/data-modules.qmd).
4. [Train and evaluate](guides/lightning.qmd): compare dispute predictions with the existing review process before adding more context.

## Proofs And Benchmarks

[Proofs](proofs.qmd) are small, controlled learning experiments on synthetic
data. Each page shows a schema, a comparison, and a recorded result for a
question such as adding values or matching unfamiliar IDs. Use them to
understand what a model can learn under the tested conditions, where information
can be lost, and which assumptions to test in your own model.

[Benchmarks](benchmarks.qmd) describe evaluations for complete workloads, from
dispute review to batch scoring. Their schemas, baseline comparisons, and
metrics connect model choices to prediction quality, review capacity, and
processing costs. Use them to plan how to judge whether a model improves your
workflow and fits its time and resource budget. Current benchmark data,
schemas, and numbers are **fictional placeholders**; no benchmark runs have
been performed.

## Go Further When You Need To

The later examples extend the transaction model in order:

| Business question | What the example adds |
| --- | --- |
| [Will this merchant be paid again?](guides/learning-from-event-data.qmd) | Payment channels, account profile context, and a second outcome learned from the same history. |
| [Which transactions and accounts need attention?](case-studies/customer-risk.qmd) | Line items inside transactions, a separate withdrawal history, and a future account-loss target alongside transaction disputes. |
| [Can unlabeled activity help?](guides/pretraining.qmd) | Reconstruction of hidden historical fields before adapting to an outcome. |
| [Can other predictors reuse the context?](core-concepts/embeddings.qmd) | Frozen transaction-history representations evaluated on separate tasks. |
| [Where else does this pattern apply?](case-studies/relational-tasks.qmd) | Purchase histories for retention, followed by other related-record applications. |

Follow [Model Structure](core-concepts/model-tree.qmd) and
[Field Interactions](guides/mechanisms/field-interactions.qmd) when you want to
understand how the model combines the evidence.

The examples use payments and accounts. The same field and branch definitions
work with other kinds of tabular and nested records.
